draft.title: Structuring a speech
card: The opening line grabs the audience's attention. It can be a surprising fact, a question or a short story.
The speaker tells the audience what the main points are and when they move on. Phrases such as "My first point is" and "Now I turn to" do this.
Each main point is explained and backed with examples, facts or stories. This makes the point clear and believable.
The close leaves the audience with something to remember. It often returns to the hook or repeats the central message in a strong final line.
draft.remember: A speech grabs attention, shows the way, backs up its points and ends strongly.

a.q: A speaker says, "I will give you three reasons. First, sleep helps learning." What is the speaker doing with the first sentence?
opts: Signposting the points that will follow
Developing a point with an example
a.why: The speaker tells the audience how the speech is organised, which is signposting. It is not development, because no example or explanation backs up a point yet.
a.clue: The speaker is telling the audience what is coming.

b.q: Priya is giving a speech on why her town needs a skate park. She has finished her opening and signposted three points. What should she do next in each main point?
opts: Explain it and support it with an example
Repeat her opening line to end the speech
List all three points again straight away
Start a new hook for the next point
b.why: After signposting, each point is developed with examples, facts or stories so the audience understands and believes it. Repeating the opening line belongs to the ending, so it is too early here.
b.clue: A point needs something to back it up.

a.best: Signposting the points that will follow

b.best: Explain it and support it with an example
